Hire Vue.js developers: vetting and interview guide

September 30, 2026

# Hire Vue.js developers: vetting and interview guide

Hire Vue.js developers in 2026: how to screen for Vue 3, Composition API, Pinia and Nuxt 4, tell three profiles apart, and ask questions that show depth.

HighCircl Editorial Team

September 30, 2026

Hire Vue.js developers: vetting and interview guide

Hire Vue.js developers in 2026: how to screen for Vue 3, Composition API, Pinia and Nuxt 4, tell three profiles apart, and ask questions that show depth.

HighCircl Editorial Team

When you hire Vue.js developers, a resume that says "five years of Vue" can mean five years of Vue 2 with the Options API and nothing else. Vue 2 reached end of life on December 31st, 2023, so that experience comes from a version that no longer gets patches. It doesn't tell you whether the person can build with the Composition API, manage state with Pinia, or ship a server-rendered Nuxt app.

This guide sits in our series Hire developers by tech stack: rates, vetting and interview guides. For Vue, most bad hires are decided before the interview, by a job spec that doesn't pin versions or rendering mode.

## Why "Vue developer" hides three different hires

Most Vue job posts are really one of three roles.

The first is the Vue 3 single-page-app engineer. They build a client-rendered app on Vue 3 with Vite, TypeScript and Pinia, usually against an API somebody else owns. The second is the Nuxt full-stack engineer, who also owns server rendering, data fetching on the server and the hydration bugs that come with both. Nuxt describes itself as a framework to build full-stack web applications and websites with Vue.js, and it expects real server-side judgment from whoever uses it. The third is the Vue plus Laravel engineer, who works across a PHP backend and a Vue frontend, often with Inertia in between.

The step most job posts skip is naming the rendering mode. Write "SPA", "SSR" or "SSG" in the ad. A candidate who has only built SPAs will read "SSR" and either self-select out or ask sharp questions, and both outcomes save you an interview.

## Vue 2 vs Vue 3 vs Nuxt versions in 2026: what to write in the job spec

Pin versions in the job spec. It costs one line and filters out mismatched resumes.

Vue 2 is finished. Commercial extended support exists through HeroDevs' Never-Ending Support, listed on the same Vue 2 page, but that's a paid patch service for legacy apps, not a reason to start anything new on Vue 2. Vue 3's current stable release is 3.5.43 (see the Vue core release list). Version 3.6 is still a release candidate (3.6.0-rc.9 was tagged the day after 3.5.43), so don't write "Vue 3.6" into a spec and don't screen for it.

Nuxt moves faster than most people expect. The current stable release is Nuxt 4.5.2, and the Nuxt roadmap states that Nuxt 3 reached end of life on 31 July 2026 and no longer receives bug fixes or security patches. It also estimates Nuxt 5 for Q4 2026. If your ad says "Nuxt 3", you're advertising an unsupported framework. Write "Nuxt 4" and ask about upgrade experience.

The migration angle is where this pays off. A candidate who has only maintained a Vue 2 app knows the old reactivity quirks, mixins and Vuex. A candidate who has done a 2-to-3 migration has met the reactivity change, replaced mixins with composables and moved a store to Pinia. Ask which one they are, and ask for the story.

## Vue vs React: what it means for hiring pool and ramp-up

Expect a smaller specialist pool than React's, which makes job-spec clarity matter more. A React posting can be vague and still get applicants. A vague Vue posting gets Vue 2 resumes, generalist frontend engineers who've touched Vue once, and Nuxt candidates when you wanted an SPA.

There's no primary source we can cite for how long a React developer takes to become productive in Vue, so we won't give a number. It's a fair option to consider a strong React engineer for a Vue codebase, and our hiring guide

Vue Vapor Mode: what it is and what changes in Vue 3.6 - DEV Community

Thiago Nunes Batista for Código ao Ponto

 Posted on Oct 6 • Originally published at codigoaoponto.com • AI-assisted 

# Vue Vapor Mode: what it is and what changes in Vue 3.6 

Vue 3.6 is not stable yet. As of October 6, 2026, the latest version is `3.6.0-rc.10` (September 30), and the stable release is still `3.5.43` (September 17). I checked both on npm and in the `vuejs/core` releases on that date.

Vue Vapor Mode is the headline feature of 3.6: a compilation mode that skips the Virtual DOM and generates code that updates the DOM directly. It is opt-in, so you pick which components use it and you don't rewrite your app. This article covers how Vapor works, how to enable it in Vue and in Nuxt 4.6, what it doesn't support yet, and when it's worth a try.

## How Vapor works 

In the traditional mode, when reactive state changes, Vue runs the render function, builds a new tree of VNodes (plain JavaScript objects that describe the UI), compares it with the previous tree, and only then touches the real DOM.

In Vapor Mode, the compiler analyzes the template and generates code that manipulates the DOM directly. Vapor components don't create VNodes or diff trees at runtime. When a reactive value changes, only the part of the DOM bound to it is updated.

According to the official Vue 3.6 release notes, the goal is a smaller baseline bundle and better performance. The same notes say Vapor reached the same level of performance as Solid and Svelte 5 in third-party benchmarks (js-framework-benchmark). As with any benchmark, the result depends on the scenario measured.

### What about Alien Signals? 

Vue 3.6 also ships a major refactor of `@vue/reactivity` based on the alien-signals library. The rc.1 notes say it improves the reactivity system's performance and memory usage. It's an internal change: `ref`, `reactive`, `computed` and `watch` keep the same API. Since it's part of Vue 3.6, you get it whether or not you use Vapor.

## How to enable Vapor Mode 

Vapor works with SFCs that use ` ` or only a template. You mark the component with the `vapor` attribute: 

```
<script setup vapor lang="ts">
import { ref } from 'vue'

const count = ref(0)
</script>

<template>
  <button @click="count++">
    count is {{ count }}
  </button>
</template>

```

Outside Nuxt, `@vitejs/plugin-vue` compiles Vapor SFCs (the plugin's changelog records Vapor component support, including template-only ones), so use a recent version.

Vue also accepts ` ` as shorthand for ` `. You can instead put the marker on the template with ` ` to compile the whole SFC in Vapor mode.

### Vapor components in an existing app 

In an app created with `createApp()`, you need to install `vaporInteropPlugin` to use Vapor components: 

```
import { createApp, vaporInteropPlugin } from 'vue'
import App from './App.vue'

createApp(App).use(vaporInteropPlugin).mount('#app')

```

With the plugin installed, Vapor and regular components can be nested inside each other. The Vue notes warn that this covers props, events and slots in standard usage, but not every edge case yet. Their advice is to keep distinct regions in the app, each in one mode, and to avoid mixed nesting where you can.

### A fully Vapor app 

If every component is Vapor, use `createVaporApp()`: 

```
import { createVaporApp } from 'vue'
import App from './App.vue'

createVaporApp(App).mount('#app')

```

The Virtual DOM runtime then stays out of the bundle. Each component still needs the `vapor` marker. Components written with render functions or JSX remain Virtual DOM components and need interop. A Vapor app can also install `vaporInteropPlugin` to accept Virtual DOM components, but that pulls the runtime back in and cuts into the bundle savings.

## Vapor in Nuxt 4.6 

Nuxt 4.6, released on October 5, 2026, supports Vapor in interop mode. The app root stays on the Virtual DOM, and you choose which components or pages use Vapor. To enable it

# Vue Components Explained: What They Are, What They Can Do, and Where Vue Stands in 2026

Kaja Grzybowska

 | Mar 13, 2025

## Table of Contents

1 Why Do Vue Components Matter for Your Product and Team?

2 How Does a Vue Component Work?

3 What Can’t a Vue Component Do on Its Own?

4 Which Vue Component Libraries Are Worth Using in 2026?

8 Is Vue a Safe Bet for Your Next Product in 2026?

2 How Does a Vue Component Work?

3 What Can’t a Vue Component Do on Its Own?

and 5 more

4 Which Vue Component Libraries Are Worth Using in 2026?

5 Do Developers Still Build Vue Components for Fun?

6 What Is the State of Vue in 2026?

7 Where Can You Learn More About Vue Components?

8 Is Vue a Safe Bet for Your Next Product in 2026?

A Vue component is a self-contained, reusable piece of a user interface, such as a button, a product card or a checkout form, that bundles its own markup, logic and styling. You build a Vue app by nesting components inside each other, much like HTML elements nest. Each piece can be built, tested and changed on its own.

This article covers what components do well, where they need help, which component libraries are worth a look, and what changed in the Vue ecosystem in 2026. It’s written for the people who make decisions about Vue projects as well as the people who write the code.

> Executive Summary
> 
> Components are the unit of work in every Vue project, so how a team builds them largely decides how fast it ships and how much the product costs to maintain. 
> 
> The core ideas are simple: props carry data in, events carry messages out, and slots pass content in. Shared state, routing and server rendering belong to tools built around components. 
> 
> In 2026, Vue gains Vapor Mode, an opt-in way to compile components without a virtual DOM for big speed and memory gains, and a much faster Rust-based toolchain led by Vite 8 and Vite+. 
> 
> Neither forces a rewrite, so teams can adopt them one component, or one project, at a time.

## Why Do Vue Components Matter for Your Product and Team?

Components turn a user interface into parts you can reuse, assign and replace, which directly lowers the cost of building and changing software.

- Reuse: a date picker built once serves every form, and fixing it once fixes it everywhere.
- Parallel work: developers can own separate components without colliding, which shortens timelines.
- Consistency: screens built from the same parts give users a coherent experience.
- Onboarding and safe change: new developers learn the product one small piece at a time, and isolated components make updates less likely to break something else.

These gains show up in business metrics, not just code reviews. When Monterail rebuilt Easyship’s website in Vue.js and Nuxt, replacing an AngularJS front end, the new site improved conversion rates by 36% and performance by 37%.

## How Does a Vue Component Work?

A Vue component keeps track of its own state and renders a piece of the page that updates automatically when that state changes. Most projects define each one in a single `.vue` file, a Single-File Component (SFC), which holds its logic, template and styles together. Here is a complete example from the Vue docs, a button that counts its own clicks:

```
<script setup>
import { ref } from 'vue'

const count = ref(0)
</script>

<template>
  <button @click="count++">You clicked me {{ count }} times.</button>
</template>

```

`count` is reactive state: when it changes, Vue updates the button for you. Place this component on a page three times and you get three independent copies, each with its own count, which is what makes components safe to reuse.

Components talk to each other through a few simple mechanisms:

- Props (data in): custom attributes that let a parent pass data to a child, such as a `title` for a `BlogPost` component. Data flows one way, so it’s always clear wher

Vue.js in 2027: The State of the Framework and What It Means for Teams - Nextage Blog

# Vue.js in 2027: The State of the Framework and What It Means for Teams Building Digital Products

By Laura Marques

24 de September de 2026

Choosing the front-end technology for a digital product is a decision that stays with a company for years. A system started today will likely still be running in 2030, and many CTOs and product managers are asking a straightforward question: is Vue.js still a safe bet for 2027 and beyond?

The data says yes, with some important caveats. Vue.js is going through one of the most technically significant periods in its history, with deep changes to its rendering engine, its tooling ecosystem and its main meta-framework, Nuxt. At the same time, it still trails React in overall usage and talent availability.

In this article, we bring together the leading market studies, the latest technical developments and the key points of attention to help you make a decision based on evidence, not hype.

The 30-second summary

- The latest stable version of Vue is 3.5; Vue 3.6, which introduces Vapor Mode, was in the release candidate stage as of this writing (September 2026).
- Vapor Mode removes the virtual DOM from the components that adopt it and delivers performance comparable to Solid and Svelte 5.
- In the State of JS 2025 survey, Vue reached 84% satisfaction, compared with 72% for React.
- The ecosystem has been renewed: Vite 8 now runs on Rolldown, a Rust-based bundler, and Nuxt 5 is on the way with the new Nitro v3 server engine.
- The main risk for companies is not Vue itself, but legacy systems still running on Vue 2 and Nuxt 3, which no longer receive support.

## Is Vue.js growing or shrinking? What the data says

Vue.js is not dying: it remains one of the highest-rated front-end frameworks on the market and keeps a stable, loyal user base. The gap with React lies in usage volume, not in perceived quality.

### Satisfaction and loyalty

The State of JavaScript 2025, one of the most respected surveys in the ecosystem, placed Vue.js in the A tier for satisfaction, with 84% of users saying they would use the framework again. Comparing it with its direct competitors puts that result into perspective:

| Technology | Satisfaction (State of JS 2025) |
| --- | --- |
| Svelte | 86% |
| Vue.js | 84% |
| Nuxt | 80% |
| React | 72% |
| Next.js | 55% |
| Angular | 48% |

The same survey highlights Vue as one of the projects whose positive perception has improved over time, which is unusual for a technology that is more than ten years old. Another notable finding is the drop in Next.js, the leading React meta-framework, whose satisfaction fell from 68% to 55% in a single year.

Community loyalty confirms this picture. According to Vue School’s 2025 review, 93% of developers plan to use Vue in their next project, and 80% say they would definitely choose it again. The same review cites 37% year-over-year growth in Vue’s weekly npm downloads, according to Evan You, the framework’s creator.

### Usage in the professional market

When the lens widens to the job market as a whole, the picture changes. In the Stack Overflow Developer Survey 2025, among professional developers, React appears with 46.9% usage, Angular with 19.8% and Vue with 18.4%, according to an analysis by Coderio.

It is worth understanding why the numbers vary so much between surveys. State of JS mainly reaches professionals who are closely engaged with the JavaScript ecosystem, while Stack Overflow covers developers across every field. The most accurate reading is this: React leads in adoption and talent supply; Vue leads in satisfaction among those who already use it.

## Vue 3.6 and Vapor Mode: the end of the virtual DOM?

Vapor Mode is a new compilation mode in Vue 3.6 that turns components into direct DOM operations, without going through the virtual DOM. It is the biggest technical change in Vue since version 3 was released in 2020.

What Is Vue Vapor Mode?

# What Is Vue Vapor Mode?

Vue Vapor Mode explained: how it compiles SFCs to direct DOM ops, what changes in Vue 3.6 RC, and key pitfalls with events and slots.

OpenReplay Team

 Sep 28, 2026 · 6 min read 

Vue Vapor Mode is a compilation mode for Vue single-file components that turns templates into direct DOM operations, so rendering and updates happen without creating or diffing a virtual DOM, which cuts baseline bundle size, update cost and memory use.

Vapor has been shown at conferences for a while now, but there is still no page about it in the Vue documentation. The detail lives in the Vue core release notes.

This article covers what Vapor Mode changes about how your components run, and where it sits in the release cycle. It also covers two behaviours in Vapor that fail silently and are easy to walk into.

## Key Takeaways

- Vapor Mode compiles Vue SFCs into direct DOM operations rather than VNode creation and diffing, which is where its smaller bundle and faster updates come from.
- Vapor Mode is feature-complete in the Vue 3.6 release candidates but is not stable: the 3.6 line is still in pre-release, with v3.6.0-rc.9 (18 September 2026) marked Pre-release on GitHub, while the Latest label stays on the 3.5 line at v3.5.43 (17 September 2026).
- Vapor is opt-in per component via ` `, ` ` or ` `, and only works on template-only SFCs and SFCs using `script setup`; the Options API is unsupported.
- `createVaporApp()` mounts a pure Vapor app that never loads the virtual DOM runtime; installing `vaporInteropPlugin` to host VDOM components pulls that runtime back in and offsets the size benefit.
- Vapor components have no VNodes and no public instance proxy, so `getCurrentInstance()` returns null, `app.config.globalProperties` does not apply, and component template refs no longer expose `$el`, `$props`, `$attrs`, `$slots` or `$refs`.

## How Does Vue Vapor Mode Work?

The v3.6.0-rc.1 release note presents Vapor as a second way to compile single-file components, aimed at a smaller starting bundle and better performance. None of it happens by default: you turn it on yourself, one component at a time, and the part of the Vue API it covers mostly behaves the way you already expect. The source you write does not change. What changes is the output: instead of a render function that produces VNodes for the runtime to diff against the previous tree, the compiler emits code that creates the nodes once and wires each reactive dependency to the specific DOM update it controls.

Removing the virtual DOM removes three costs at once. The diffing runtime itself never has to ship in a pure Vapor app, so the baseline bundle is smaller. Updates skip VNode allocation and tree comparison, so a change to one ref touches one text node or one attribute. And because no shadow tree is retained between renders, the per-component memory footprint drops.

The component itself looks like ordinary Composition API code:

```
<script setup vapor>
import { ref, computed } from 'vue'

const count = ref(0)
const doubled = computed(() => count.value * 2)
</script>

<template>
  <button @click="count++">{{ count }} / {{ doubled }}</button>
</template>
```

Only the `vapor` attribute differs from the same component compiled in VDOM mode.

## Release Status: Feature-Complete, Not Stable

Vapor Mode has not shipped in a stable Vue release. On the vuejs/core releases list, the 3.6 line is still in release candidates: v3.6.0-rc.9, published 18 September 2026, carries the Pre-release label, while the Latest label belongs to v3.5.43, published 17 September 2026. npm agrees: the `latest` dist-tag on the `vue` package points at 3.5.43, and the release candidates sit behind the separate `rc` tag. There is no 3.6.0 stable tag.

# Vue 3.6.0-rc.11

By BIOS Founding Team

The latest release candidate adds one feature: Vapor slot content can now transition inside a VDOM Transition. It also has about 60 bug fixes, mainly in the Vapor compiler and runtime.

These include rejecting Vapor scripts without script setup, v-model on const bindings, hydration, teleport and VDOM interop. Stable Vue 3.6.0 is still pending.

Full details: https://github.com/vuejs/core/releases/tag/v3.6.0-rc.11
